summary.text: An accretion disk is a structure formed by diffuse material in orbital motion around a massive central body, most frequently a star.
Friction and other forces make the orbiting material spiral inward, and as it is compressed and heated it emits electromagnetic radiation.
Disks of young stars and protostars radiate in the infrared, while those around neutron stars and black holes radiate in the X-ray part of the spectrum.

facts.label: Energy conversion
facts.value: 10 to over 40 percent of mass, versus 0.7 for fusion

facts.label: Companion output
facts.value: Often gives rise to astrophysical jets

facts.label: Planet-forming type
facts.value: Disks around T Tauri or Herbig stars are protoplanetary

items.prompt: A grain in an accretion disk rubs against its neighbours in turbulent flow. What happens to its orbit over time?

options.label: It spirals outward because friction speeds it up
It loses angular momentum and drifts inward
It stays in exactly the same orbit forever
It stops orbiting and freezes in place

items.explain: Frictional heating radiates energy away and reduces the particle's angular momentum, which allows the particle to drift inward.

items.prompt: A spinning star-and-disk system needs to get rid of its spin without losing much mass. What do such disks often produce that does this efficiently?

options.label: Astrophysical jets from near the central object
A second, larger disk around the first
Bursts of visible light from the disk's edge
A ring of planets that carries the spin away

items.explain: Disks very often give rise to jets, which are an efficient way for the star-disk system to shed angular momentum without losing too much mass.

items.prompt: Astronomers observe two disks: one around a newborn protostar and one just outside a black hole. How should their radiation differ?

options.label: Both radiate only in visible light
The protostar's disk radiates in X-rays, the black hole's in the infrared
Neither gives off radiation of any kind
The protostar's disk radiates in the infrared, the black hole's in X-rays

items.explain: Accretion disks of young stars and protostars radiate in the infrared, while those around neutron stars and black holes radiate in X-rays.

items.prompt: In a close pair of stars, gas flows from a swollen companion toward the denser partner. Why does it form a disk instead of falling straight in?

options.label: The gas is too cold to move in a straight line
The partner's magnetic field bends the gas into a ring
Angular momentum conservation blocks a straight path
The companion pushes the gas sideways with a jet

items.explain: Angular momentum conservation prevents a straight flow from one star to the other, so an accretion disk forms instead.

items.prompt: Which process turns a larger share of an object's mass into energy, and roughly how much larger?

options.label: Accretion, which converts about 10 to over 40 percent of mass versus around 0.7 percent for fusion
Fusion, which converts about 10 to over 40 percent of mass versus around 0.7 percent for accretion
They convert nearly the same share
Neither converts any of the object's mass

items.explain: Accretion can convert about 10 percent to over 40 percent of the mass of an object into energy, compared with around 0.7 percent for nuclear fusion.

items.prompt: Why are disks around T Tauri and Herbig stars called protoplanetary disks?

options.label: They are made of planets that have already formed
They orbit planets instead of stars
They are thought to be the forerunners of planetary systems
They radiate only in the X-ray part of the spectrum

items.explain: These disks are called protoplanetary because they are thought to be the progenitors of planetary systems.
